claims.text: Rapid quenching from high temperature followed by subcritical annealing promotes nanoscale phase separation in Fe-Co-Mn-Cr-Ni high-entropy alloys.
The nanoscale phase separation creates magnetically distinct clusters.
The magnetically distinct clusters are embedded in a magnetically softer continuous matrix.
Nanoscale magnetic heterogeneity enhances local magnetic exchange interactions.
Nanoscale magnetic heterogeneity enhances magnetostructural coupling.
Enhanced local exchange and magnetostructural coupling enable a sharp field-induced magnetic transition at low applied fields.
The engineered heterogeneity produces a stronger magnetocaloric response at low applied fields than a uniform microstructure.
Interfaces generated by nanoscale phase separation improve thermal conduction.
Interfaces generated by nanoscale phase separation limit magnetic hysteresis.
The proposed nanoscale heterogeneity maintains mechanical stability.
The thermally processed samples will exhibit sharper magnetic transitions than the uniform baseline.
The thermally processed samples will exhibit a faster thermal response during magnetic cycling than the uniform baseline.
The thermally processed samples will exhibit lower hysteresis than the uniform baseline.
Quenching from approximately 1200°C and annealing at 600–700°C for 1–3 hours can produce the targeted nanoscale phase separation without excessive coarsening.
The hypothesis ceases to apply if the separated phases coarsen excessively.
A Fe-Co-Mn-Cr-Ni alloy processed without rapid quenching and controlled annealing will lack nanoscale phase separation.
